In mathematics, '''inertial manifolds''' are concerned with the long term behavior of the solutions of [[dissipative]] [[dynamical system]]s.  Inertial manifolds are finite-dimensional, smooth, [[invariant manifold]]s that contain the global [[attractor]] and attract all solutions [[exponential growth|exponentially]] quickly.  Since an inertial manifold is [[Dimension (vector space)|finite-dimensional]] even if the original system is infinite-dimensional, and because most of the dynamics for the system takes place on the inertial manifold,  studying the dynamics on an inertial manifold produces a considerable simplification in the study of the dynamics of the original system.<ref name="Temam1990">R. Temam. Inertial manifolds. ''Mathematical Intelligencer'', 12:68–74, 1990</ref>

In many physical applications, inertial manifolds express an interaction law between the small and large wavelength structures.  Some say that the small wavelengths are enslaved by the large (e.g. [[Synergetics (Haken)|synergetics]]).  Inertial manifolds may also appear as [[slow manifold]]s common in meteorology, or as the [[center manifold]] in any [[bifurcation theory|bifurcation]].  Computationally, numerical schemes for [[partial differential equation]]s seek to capture the long term dynamics and so such numerical schemes form an approximate inertial manifold.

==Introductory Example==

Consider the dynamical system in just two variables&nbsp;<math>p(t)</math> and&nbsp;<math>q(t)</math> and with parameter&nbsp;<math>a</math>:<ref>{{cite journal | last=Roberts | first=A. J. | title=Simple examples of the derivation of amplitude equations for systems of equations possessing bifurcations | journal=Journal of the Australian Mathematical Society, Series B | publisher=Cambridge University Press (CUP) | volume=27 | issue=1 | year=1985 | issn=0334-2700 | doi=10.1017/s0334270000004756 | pages=48–65| doi-access=free }}</ref>
:<math>\frac{dp}{dt}=ap-pq\,,\qquad \frac{dq}{dt}=-q+p^2-2q^2.</math>
* It possesses the one dimensional inertial manifold&nbsp;<math>\mathcal M</math> of <math>q=p^2/(1+2a)</math> (a parabola).
* This manifold is invariant under the dynamics because on the manifold&nbsp;<math>\mathcal M</math>
:&nbsp;<math>\frac{dq}{dt}
=\frac{d}{dt}\frac{p^2}{1+2a}
=\frac{2p\frac{dp}{dt}}{1+2a}
=\frac{2ap^2}{1+2a}-\frac{2p^4}{(1+2a)^2}</math> which is the same as
:&nbsp;<math>-q+p^2-2q^2
=-\frac{p^2}{1+2a}+p^2-2\left(\frac{p^2}{1+2a}\right)^2
=\frac{2ap^2}{1+2a}-\frac{2p^4}{(1+2a)^2}.</math>
* The manifold&nbsp;<math>\mathcal M</math> attracts all trajectories in some finite domain around the origin because near the origin&nbsp;<math>\frac{dq}{dt}\approx -q</math>  (although the strict definition below requires attraction from all initial conditions).

Hence the long term behavior of the original two dimensional dynamical system is given by the 'simpler' one dimensional dynamics on the inertial manifold&nbsp;<math>\mathcal M</math>, namely&nbsp;<math>\frac{dp}{dt}=ap-\frac1{1+2a}p^3</math>.

==Definition==

Let <math>u(t)</math> denote a solution of a dynamical system.  The solution&nbsp;<math>u(t)</math> may be an evolving vector in <math>H=\mathbb R^n</math> or may be an evolving function in an infinite-dimensional [[Banach space]]&nbsp;<math>H</math>.

In many cases of interest the evolution of&nbsp;<math>u(t)</math> is determined as the solution of a differential equation in&nbsp;<math>H</math>, say <math>{du}/{dt}=F(u(t))</math> with initial value <math>u(0)=u_0</math>.
In any case, we assume the solution of the dynamical system can be written in terms of a [[semigroup]] operator, or [[state transition matrix]], <math>S:H\to H</math> such that <math>u(t)=S(t)u_0</math> for all times <math>t\geq0</math> and all initial values&nbsp;<math>u_0</math>.
In some situations we might consider only discrete values of time as in the dynamics of a map.

An '''inertial manifold'''<ref name="Temam1990"/> for a dynamical semigroup&nbsp;<math>S(t)</math> is a smooth [[manifold]]&nbsp;<math>\mathcal M</math> such that
# <math>\mathcal M</math> is of finite dimension,
# <math>S(t)\mathcal M\subset\mathcal M</math> for all times&nbsp;<math>t\geq0</math>,
# <math>\mathcal M</math> attracts all solutions exponentially quickly, that is, for every initial value&nbsp;<math>u_0\in H</math> there exist constants&nbsp;<math>c_j>0</math> such that <math>\text{dist}(S(t)u_0,\mathcal M)\leq c_1e^{-c_2t}</math>.

The restriction of the differential equation&nbsp;<math>du/dt=F(u)</math> to the inertial manifold&nbsp;<math>\mathcal M</math> is therefore a well defined finite-dimensional system called the '''inertial system'''.<ref name="Temam1990"/>
Subtly, there is a difference between a manifold being attractive, and solutions on the manifold being attractive.
Nonetheless, under appropriate conditions the inertial system possesses so-called '''asymptotic completeness''':<ref>{{cite journal | last=Robinson | first=James C | title=The asymptotic completeness of inertial manifolds | journal=Nonlinearity | publisher=IOP Publishing | volume=9 | issue=5 | date=1996-09-01 | issn=0951-7715 | doi=10.1088/0951-7715/9/5/013 | bibcode=1996Nonli...9.1325R | pages=1325–1340| s2cid=250890338 }}</ref> that is, every solution of the differential equation has a companion solution lying in&nbsp;<math>\mathcal M</math> and producing the same behavior for large time; in mathematics, for all&nbsp;<math>u_0</math> there exists&nbsp;<math>v_0\in\mathcal M</math> and possibly a time shift&nbsp;<math>\tau\geq0</math> such that <math>\text{dist}(S(t)u_0,S(t+\tau)v_0)\to0</math> as&nbsp;<math>t\to\infty</math>.

Researchers in the 2000s generalized such inertial manifolds to time dependent (nonautonomous) and/or stochastic dynamical systems (e.g.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Schmalfuss | first1=Björn | last2=Schneider | first2=Klaus R. | title=Invariant Manifolds for Random Dynamical Systems with Slow and Fast Variables | journal=Journal of Dynamics and Differential Equations | publisher=Springer Science and Business Media LLC | volume=20 | issue=1 | date=2007-09-18 | issn=1040-7294 | doi=10.1007/s10884-007-9089-7 | bibcode=2008JDDE...20..133S | pages=133–164| s2cid=123477654 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1=Pötzsche | first1=Christian | last2=Rasmussen | first2=Martin | title=Computation of nonautonomous invariant and inertial manifolds | journal=Numerische Mathematik | publisher=Springer Science and Business Media LLC | volume=112 | issue=3 | date=2009-02-18 | issn=0029-599X | doi=10.1007/s00211-009-0215-9 | pages=449–483| s2cid=6111461 | url=https://opus.bibliothek.uni-augsburg.de/opus4/files/602/mpreprint_07_041.pdf }}</ref>)

==Existence==

Existence results that have been proved address inertial manifolds that are expressible as a graph.<ref name="Temam1990"/>
The governing differential equation is rewritten more specifically in the form <math>du/dt+Au+f(u)=0</math> for unbounded self-adjoint closed operator&nbsp;<math>A</math> with domain&nbsp;<math>D(A)\subset H</math>, and nonlinear operator&nbsp;<math>f:D(A)\to H</math>.
Typically, elementary spectral theory gives an [[orthonormal basis]] of&nbsp;<math>H</math> consisting of eigenvectors&nbsp;<math> v_j</math>: <math>Av_j=\lambda_jv_j</math>, <math>j=1,2,\ldots</math>, for ordered eigenvalues <math>0<\lambda_1\leq \lambda_2\leq\cdots</math>.

For some given number&nbsp;<math>m</math> of modes, <math>P</math>&nbsp;denotes the projection of&nbsp;<math>H</math> onto the space spanned by&nbsp;<math>v_1,\ldots,v_m</math>, and <math>Q=I-P</math>&nbsp;denotes the orthogonal projection onto the space spanned by&nbsp;<math>v_{m+1},v_{m+2},\ldots</math>.
We look for an inertial manifold expressed as the graph&nbsp;<math>\Phi:PH\to QH</math>.
For this graph to exist the most restrictive requirement is the '''spectral gap condition'''<ref name="Temam1990"/>&nbsp;<math>\lambda_{m+1}-\lambda_m \geq c(\sqrt{\lambda_{m+1}}+\sqrt{\lambda_m})</math> where the constant&nbsp;<math>c</math> depends upon the system.
This spectral gap condition requires that the spectrum of&nbsp;<math>A</math> must contain large gaps to be guaranteed of existence.

==Approximate inertial manifolds==
Several methods are proposed to construct approximations to
inertial manifolds,<ref name="Temam1990"/> including the
so-called ''intrinsic low-dimensional manifolds''.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Maas | first1=U. | last2=Pope | first2=S.B. | title=Simplifying chemical kinetics: Intrinsic low-dimensional manifolds in composition space | journal=Combustion and Flame | publisher=Elsevier BV | volume=88 | issue=3–4 | year=1992 | issn=0010-2180 | doi=10.1016/0010-2180(92)90034-m | pages=239–264}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1=Bykov | first1=Viatcheslav | last2=Goldfarb | first2=Igor | last3=Gol'dshtein | first3=Vladimir | last4=Maas | first4=Ulrich | title=On a modified version of ILDM approach: asymptotic analysis based on integral manifolds | journal=IMA Journal of Applied Mathematics | publisher=Oxford University Press (OUP) | volume=71 | issue=3 | date=2006-06-01 | issn=1464-3634 | doi=10.1093/imamat/hxh100 | pages=359–382| url=https://publikationen.bibliothek.kit.edu/1000010843/794465 }}</ref>

The most popular way to approximate follows from the
existence of a graph.
Define the&nbsp;<math>m</math> ''slow variables''&nbsp;<math>p(t)=Pu(t)</math>, and the 'infinite'
''fast variables''&nbsp;<math>q(t)=Qu(t)</math>.
Then project the differential equation
<math>du/dt+Au+f(u)=0</math> onto both&nbsp;<math>PH</math>
and&nbsp;<math>QH</math> to obtain the coupled system
<math>dp/dt+Ap+Pf(p+q)=0</math> and
<math>dq/dt+Aq+Qf(p+q)=0</math>.

For trajectories on the graph of an inertial
manifold&nbsp;<math>M</math>, the fast
variable&nbsp;<math>q(t)=\Phi(p(t))</math>.
Differentiating and using the coupled system form gives the
differential equation for the graph:
:<math>-\frac{d\Phi}{dp}\left[Ap+Pf(p+\Phi(p))\right]
+A\Phi(p)+Qf(p+\Phi(p))=0.</math>
This differential equation is typically solved approximately
in an asymptotic expansion in 'small'&nbsp;<math>p</math> to
give an invariant manifold model,<ref>{{cite journal | last=Roberts | first=A. J. | title=The Utility of an Invariant Manifold Description of the Evolution of a Dynamical System | journal=SIAM Journal on Mathematical Analysis | publisher=Society for Industrial & Applied Mathematics (SIAM) | volume=20 | issue=6 | year=1989 | issn=0036-1410 | doi=10.1137/0520094 | pages=1447–1458}}</ref>
or a nonlinear [[Galerkin method]],<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Foias | first1=C. | last2=Jolly | first2=M.S. | last3=Kevrekidis | first3=I.G. | last4=Sell | first4=G.R. | last5=Titi | first5=E.S. | title=On the computation of inertial manifolds | journal=Physics Letters A | publisher=Elsevier BV | volume=131 | issue=7–8 | year=1988 | issn=0375-9601 | doi=10.1016/0375-9601(88)90295-2 | bibcode=1988PhLA..131..433F | pages=433–436}}</ref>
both of which use a global basis whereas the so-called
''holistic discretisation'' uses a local basis.<ref>{{cite journal|first1=A. J.|last1=Roberts|title=A holistic finite difference approach models linear dynamics consistently|journal=Mathematics of Computation|volume=72|issue=241|pages=247–262|date=2002-06-04|citeseerx=10.1.1.207.4820|doi=10.1090/S0025-5718-02-01448-5|s2cid=11525980}}</ref>
Such approaches to approximation of inertial manifolds are
very closely related to approximating [[center manifold]]s
for which a web service exists to construct approximations
for systems input by a
user.<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://www.maths.adelaide.edu.au/anthony.roberts/gencm.php | title=Construct centre manifolds of ordinary or delay differential equations (autonomous)}}</ref>
